doc.title: Tyner McCoy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Eric Dolphy on Africa/Brass; Bobby Hutcherson
summary: Tyner clarifies Dolphy's role on the Africa/Brass session; Brown and Aisha speak of Dolphy and Bobby Hutcherson.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: I’m going to just backtrack because we are talking about orchestration and arranging and I know that Eric Dolphy was credited for arranging the Africa/Brass session when in fact I know that it was your arrangement and Eric did the orchestration based on your arrangement so just wanted to verify, is that the case?

Yeah he didn’t write arrangements for me, but he had good ideas if I wanted to know something about flute or anything, I could ask him and the range--I never wanted a guy to struggle you know, playing two or three octaves above what he could do. Eric had a lot of experience playing different kinds of music and I tried to get guys that had that kind of ability, they play other music that taught them something and I would ask them, “If I do that, and I put it a C above C, how high or whatever” and he would tell me one way or another whether or not that would be comfortable.
Now we interviewed Bobby earlier and he talked about Eric because they’re both from Los Angeles

We’re going to talk about that, but could we talk a little bit more, because Bobby talked very highly of Eric as a person, not just as a musician, although that was above any critique. I mean he was definitely a musician’s musician, but as a person that seemed to impress Bobby and I think John talked about Eric, about his personality. Did you have a good-
Yeah he had a sense of humor as well. He was a nice man, really really good man and a great musician.
Well you know I’m from California, we’re (Ken and I) from California so Eric, you know Eric and Mingus and Ornette you know those are our folks. You got Philadelphia, that’s all we got is California.

Let me just pull that out for the record (Manhattan Moods), this is one of my favorites. I play along with this record because there is no drummer, I get to be the drummer with Bobby Hutcherson and McCoy Tyner.
Oh yeah, Bobby. Look at that smile! That smile is captivating.
